channel.title: The Wall Street Journal - CIO Journal
channel.description: Technology leadership and enterprise technology news from CIO Journal

item.title: Nvidia Board Must Craft Epic Job Description for New CEO
item.description:
In the Morning Download, Steven Rosenbush argues that Nvidia's board faces a daunting search after Jensen Huang resigned following two extramarital affairs, one of them with a suspected Chinese spy, since the company needs a successor with Jobs-level instincts for innovation and sales who can also instill greater calm and discipline and take "a less-imperial approach to leadership." Longtime CFO Colette Kress was named interim CEO, and Nvidia stock dropped more than 7% before the opening bell while other chip stocks slipped far less. The newsletter also notes that Nvidia quit reporting its Singapore revenue separately soon after cutting off Megaspeed, the Singapore firm tied to the espionage scandal, and has declined to say whether the two moves were connected.


Sources:

  • Nvidia Board Must Craft Epic Job Description for New CEO - wsj.com
item.dc:creator: Steven Rosenbush

item.title: AI Startup LangChain More Than Doubles Its Valuation to $3 Billion
item.description:
LangChain, whose software helps developers build AI apps and agents, raised $300 million in a round led by Alphabet's CapitalG that values it at $3 billion, more than twice its valuation from October of last year, Belle Lin reports. The money will go toward expanding LangSmith, the startup's platform for monitoring, evaluating and deploying agents, as many enterprises hold back on agents until governance is in place; "The agent's behavior is the hard part to control," said co-founder and CEO Harrison Chase. CapitalG partner Mo Jomaa called the field "an insanely competitive market" in which big players try to lock customers into their own ecosystems, and the three-year-old company plans to grow from 435 full-time staff to 850 by the end of next year.


Sources:

  • AI Startup LangChain More Than Doubles Its Valuation to $3 Billion - wsj.com
item.dc:creator: Belle Lin

item.title: AI Is Testing the Limits of Corporate Governance
item.description:
Drawing on remarks at the WSJ Leadership Institute's board summit in Palm Beach, Steven Rosenbush writes that directors regard AI as here to stay and want governance to keep pace, with SLB and Adidas board member Jing Ulrich saying "Technology changes faster than governance" and ExCo Group's Shellye Archambeau noting that the talk has shifted from cutting heads to driving strategy. GM and Procter & Gamble director Joe Jimenez asked how the next generation of leaders will develop if AI eliminates or radically reshapes entry-level jobs. The newsletter also notes that CoreWeave beat revenue expectations and raised its guidance, and that Wachtell Lipton will lead an independent probe into whether Nvidia was targeted by foreign espionage.


Sources:

  • AI Is Testing the Limits of Corporate Governance - wsj.com
item.dc:creator: Steven Rosenbush

item.title: Why Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Is Unique
item.description:
Steven Rosenbush writes that Nvidia's board may test whether anyone is truly irreplaceable, crediting Jensen Huang's founder vision for turning an early bet on videogame graphics chips into a $4.5 trillion AI powerhouse while warning that Huang's misstep has put the company "in a uniquely precarious position." Some attendees at the WSJ Leadership Institute's board summit questioned whether Nvidia's directors moved too quickly to protect Huang over his relationship with a Singapore-based data center executive whom U.S. officials believe fed intelligence to China, and the newsletter notes the chip maker has no chairman, no succession plan and, as of last spring, three of its 10 independent directors in their seats for 25 years or more. It also covers President Trump's defense of Huang ("I really believe him") and several tech leaders' plans to push ahead with AI whatever happens to regulation after the election.


Sources:

  • Why Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Is Unique - wsj.com
item.dc:creator: Steven Rosenbush

item.title: Enterprises Say AI Regulation Won’t Stop Corporate Innovation
item.description:
Corporate tech leaders who spoke with the WSJ Leadership Institute say they will press ahead with AI whatever rules emerge under Democratic control of Congress and state offices, citing their own internal guardrails and the view that today's models already do what they need. Sutherland CIO Doug Gilbert said everyday work has an "extremely low" need for the most powerful frontier models, and Intuit CTO Alex Balazs said his company is investing heavily in its AI harness, the software layer that runs models and lets businesses mix providers. Many of the executives expect AI policy to stay at the state level for now, a patchwork that Appian CEO Matt Calkins warned could be "irregular across the nation".


Sources:

  • Enterprises Say AI Regulation Won’t Stop Corporate Innovation - wsj.com
item.dc:creator: Belle Lin

item.title: Ready to Start Your Next Car Lease With an AI Chatbot? BMW Wants to Help.
item.description:
This Morning Download leads with BMW's new U.S. ChatGPT app, which lets shoppers check local inventory, configure a vehicle, build a lease financing package and book a test drive, though the lease itself must still be completed at a dealer. BMW of North America marketing vice president Leigh Moynihan called the app "a must do" as more customers research cars with chatbots, and North America chief customer officer Andreas Walter said the team tested heavily to make sure "there's no hallucination going on" in financial answers. The newsletter also covers the Nvidia board's probe of reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a suspected Chinese spy, and a jobs report showing a 70,000-job gain in professional and business services.


Sources:

  • Ready to Start Your Next Car Lease With an AI Chatbot? BMW Wants to Help. - wsj.com

item.title: OpenAI Bolsters Cyber Defenses
item.description:
This Morning Download leads with OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber model, which the company says was trained with alignment as a central focus to keep it within authorized scope and paired with stronger safeguards against misuse, including attempts to distill its models; OpenAI reports a 51% relative improvement over GPT-5.6 Cyber on the ExploitGym benchmark. "It is clear that we have a limited window to use frontier models to secure software," the company said, while JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon recently called cyber threats "our biggest risk". The newsletter also covers Thursday's tech selloff, in which the Magnificent Seven lost about $1 trillion in market value, and reports that three major investors now expect Anthropic's planned IPO valuation of about $1.5 trillion will probably have to come down.


Sources:

  • OpenAI Bolsters Cyber Defenses - wsj.com
item.dc:creator: Steven Rosenbush

item.title: What AI Leaders Can Learn from the Midterms
item.description:
In this Morning Download, Steven Rosenbush argues that the AI industry's troubles with data center opposition and broader AI anxiety are a political problem, and offers lessons from the midterms: situational awareness, openness to dissent and compromise, clarity, accountability and explaining the larger mission. Meta President Dina Powell McCormick said data centers are "going to be harder" to build after the election, voters sided against data centers in every one of 41 local ballot measures but one in Harwood, North Dakota, and PitchBook reported global AI venture funding fell 43.4% in the third quarter. Barclays analyst Andrew Keches noted that operators already running or powered up gain "scarcity value" if construction slows, and Amazon and Microsoft rallied more than 6% on Wednesday.


Sources:

  • What AI Leaders Can Learn from the Midterms - wsj.com
item.dc:creator: Steven Rosenbush

item.title: Mercedes Gives Its Cars an AI Upgrade
item.description:
Mercedes-Benz has begun rolling out conversational AI in some North American cars using on-device foundation models from MIT spinout Liquid AI, which handle routine requests like navigation, seat settings and calls, and pass broader questions such as restaurant tips to larger cloud models, with a fleetwide rollout planned for the second quarter of 2027 at no extra charge. Mercedes-Benz North America CEO Jason Hoff cites privacy, speed, offline operation and better handling of accents, calling the effort "more about the user interface and user experience inside the vehicle" than autonomy. Cars are an especially strong case for on-device AI because they can't count on a cloud connection, Bousquette notes, while Gartner's Craig Roth says most enterprise applications still default to cloud models, even as Gartner projects on-device models will handle 30% of user-initiated enterprise AI tasks by 2029.


Sources:

  • Mercedes Gives Its Cars an AI Upgrade - wsj.com
item.dc:creator: Isabelle Bousquette

item.title: Democratic Wave Changes AI Policy Calculus
item.description:
In this Morning Download, Steven Rosenbush writes that Democratic control of the House and Senate makes the long-held assumption that Congress would pass nothing on tech look less certain, though it is too early to know what might emerge on data center construction or AI safety, while analyst Dan Ives called the midterm "a seismic shift" likely to slow the planned buildout of 800 to 1,000 U.S. data centers. Newly elected Democratic governors in Texas, Ohio and Georgia have backed full or conditional data center moratoriums, with Bloomberg estimating about 13 GW of Texas capacity immediately exposed. The newsletter also notes AMD's $13.4 billion quarter, driven by data center GPU sales, and Google's decision to switch off its AI tools by default on K-12 student accounts.


Sources:

  • Democratic Wave Changes AI Policy Calculus - wsj.com
item.dc:creator: Steven Rosenbush

item.title: AI’s Most Wanted Hire Gets a Big Raise
item.description:
In this Morning Download, Tom Loftus writes that the forward-deployed engineer has gone "from hired gun to the hottest hire in tech" as Christian & Timbers data shows elite FDEs earning $586,000 to $1.45 million a year while Gartner finds 44% of CEOs struggle to show financial returns from AI. Enterprises are now putting FDEs on their own payrolls, setting off a scramble with tech companies and consulting firms as OpenAI and Anthropic launch dedicated FDE services firms. The newsletter also covers Palantir's 96% third-quarter revenue jump to $2.31 billion, led by U.S. commercial sales, and Apple's 12% September-quarter revenue gain alongside projections that fell short of estimates.


Sources:

  • AI’s Most Wanted Hire Gets a Big Raise - wsj.com
item.dc:creator: Tom Loftus

item.title: Demand for Forward-Deployed Engineers Is Leading to $1.5 Million Paychecks
item.description:
Executive search firm Christian & Timbers found that elite forward-deployed engineers, those who have put agentic AI into production with at least $10 million in documented impact and led FDE teams, now earn $586,000 to $1.45 million a year, and about 80% are current or former Palantir engineers. Target, Barclays and American Express have posted FDE listings, and founder Jeff Christian said "Every company is thinking, 'We got to do this ourselves,'" as businesses bring the role in-house to keep their data private. Only about 2,000 of the roughly 17,000 U.S. FDEs count as elite, setting up a three-way tug-of-war among enterprises, tech companies and consulting firms, and Snowflake's Jonathan Beaulier called hiring them "massively hard."


Sources:

  • Demand for Forward-Deployed Engineers Is Leading to $1.5 Million Paychecks - wsj.com

item.title: CIOs Say Companies Tighten Focus on AI Outcomes
item.description:
In this Morning Download, Tom Loftus reports that the WSJ Leadership Institute found no slowdown in enterprise AI demand after last week's tech selloff, though CIOs expect a sharper focus on outcomes, clearer business cases and shorter payback periods. Grant Thornton CIO Mike Kempe called building and applying AI "two very different economic models," Smartsheet's Ravi Soin said "Spending will not cease, but it will become more selective," and Bristol Myers Squibb's Greg Meyers said falling vendor valuations can increase buyers' leverage in contract negotiations. The newsletter also covers SemiAnalysis' new GDPx industry benchmark, topped by Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5, and OpenAI securing about $11 billion of a $30 billion round at a $1.25 trillion valuation.


Sources:

  • CIOs Say Companies Tighten Focus on AI Outcomes - wsj.com
item.dc:creator: Tom Loftus

item.title: Enterprise AI Is on the Ballot Too
item.description:
In this Morning Download, Isabelle Bousquette argues that midterm-season tech policy fights could reach CIOs' AI plans even if aimed at frontier developers, citing Cato Institute fellow Jennifer Huddleston's warning that rules meant for AI companies "are going to impact an array of industries," from chatbot age verification to a state-by-state legal patchwork. Guardrails Alliance director Shaunna Thomas adds that labor proposals and voter appetite for job guarantees could shape how companies pair AI agents with human workers. The newsletter also notes that cloud revenue grew strongly amid a week of tech earnings selloffs, and that Mistral released its open-weight Mistral Large 4, which it pitches for coding and cybersecurity.


Sources:

  • Enterprise AI Is on the Ballot Too - wsj.com
